"executive_summary": "This paper proposes laboratory experiments to search for spatial or temporal variation of the electron-to-proton mass ratio, mu, defined as the ratio of the electron mass to the proton mass. The theoretical motivation comes from string-inspired models that predict variation in mu should be larger than variation in the fine structure constant by a factor of approximately 30. The authors demonstrate that molecular vibrational levels can be highly sensitive to changes in mu, and that pairs of closely-spaced levels can enhance sensitivity relative to the level splitting. They show spectroscopic data verifying a near-degeneracy in the ground vibronic levels of cesium dimer, Cs2. The system is attractive because it has two low-lying overlapping potentials with incommensurate vibrational splittings, a large mass yielding high density of states, and extremely long radiative lifetimes exceeding one second. The authors experimentally determine positions of deeply bound a3Sigma-plus-u levels using two-color photoassociation spectroscopy with ultracold cesium atoms at temperatures around 100 microkelvin. They observe multiple sublevels for several vibrational levels with binding energies between 400 and 1500 GHz, and identify a degeneracy between a3Sigma-plus-u and X1Sigma-plus-g levels. Based on conservative assumptions of one measurement every 2 seconds with signal-to-noise of 100, they estimate that a fractional change of delta mu over mu less than or equal to 10 to the power of negative 17 could be detected in approximately one day, requiring only about ten times less accuracy than the best atomic clocks. Executive Summary
This paper proposes laboratory experiments to search for spatial or temporal variation of the electron-to-proton mass ratio, mu, defined as the ratio of the electron mass to the proton mass. The theoretical motivation comes from string-inspired models that predict variation in mu should be larger than variation in the fine structure constant by a factor of approximately 30. The authors demonstrate that molecular vibrational levels can be highly sensitive to changes in mu, and that pairs of closely-spaced levels can enhance sensitivity relative to the level splitting. They show spectroscopic data verifying a near-degeneracy in the ground vibronic levels of cesium dimer, Cs2. The system is attractive because it has two low-lying overlapping potentials with incommensurate vibrational splittings, a large mass yielding high density of states, and extremely long radiative lifetimes exceeding one second. The authors experimentally determine positions of deeply bound a3Sigma-plus-u levels using two-color photoassociation spectroscopy with ultracold cesium atoms at temperatures around 100 microkelvin. They observe multiple sublevels for several vibrational levels with binding energies between 400 and 1500 GHz, and identify a degeneracy between a3Sigma-plus-u and X1Sigma-plus-g levels. Based on conservative assumptions of one measurement every 2 seconds with signal-to-noise of 100, they estimate that a fractional change of delta mu over mu less than or equal to 10 to the power of negative 17 could be detected in approximately one day, requiring only about ten times less accuracy than the best atomic clocks. The paper argues this system is promising for future searches for small variations in mu.

Research Context
The variation of fundamental constants has generated intense interest from string-inspired models. These models can include extra dimensions and light scalar fields that change apparent constant values. Such fields are candidates to explain the observed dark energy dominating the universe. Measurements can only detect variation in dimensionless constants on general principles. Most attention has focused on possible variation of the fine structure constant alpha. Variations in alpha are no more likely than in any other fundamental dimensionless parameter. Within grand unified theories, variation in mu should exceed variation in alpha by a factor of approximately 30. Study of mu is a potentially more sensitive method to observe any variation of constants. The most sensitive tests for variation in mu have come from examining molecular spectra from cosmologically distant sources. Systematic errors in these measurements can be significant and difficult to eliminate. A new type of laboratory experiment is proposed to search for variation of mu with high sensitivity.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether molecular vibrational levels can be highly sensitive to changes in mu. The hypothesis is that pairs of closely-spaced levels can enhance sensitivity relative to the level splitting. The predicted outcome is that the splitting between pairs of levels in Cs2 could be measured to sense a fractional change of delta mu over mu less than or equal to 10 to the power of negative 17. The sensitivity is governed by the absolute change of the energy splitting with respect to a fractional change in mu. The primary figure of merit is the ratio of the energy sensitivity to the linewidth. The secondary figure of merit is the relative change of the splitting, which matters because the splitting must be measured with respect to a reference clock. The analysis assumes both the electron mass and alpha remain constant, so a change in mu corresponds to a variation of the proton mass. The predicted outcome is that the maximum value of the energy sensitivity is obtained for levels with energy approximately equal to three-quarters of the dissociation limit. The predicted outcome is that the energy sensitivity is only slightly diminished from its expected value in the harmonic approximation. The predicted outcome is that a search for variation of mu will be most sensitive when using nearly-degenerate levels lying as close as possible to the a state minimum.

Methodological Details
The study analyzes shifts in molecular energy levels when mu changes, assuming both the electron mass and alpha remain constant. The vibrational energy levels are approximated via the WKB quantization condition involving the internuclear distance. The reduced mass of the nuclei is proportional to the proton mass and appears in the quantization integral. The energy sensitivity is derived by varying the quantization condition with respect to both mu and the vibrational quantum number. The density of states is defined as the inverse of the derivative of the energy with respect to the vibrational quantum number. Near its minimum, a typical potential is harmonic with the energy sensitivity having a v-fold enhancement for the vth vibrational level. The maximum value of the energy sensitivity is obtained for levels with energy approximately equal to three-quarters of the dissociation limit. The molecule Cs2 has two low-lying overlapping potentials: the deep X1Sigma-plus-g ground state and the shallower a3Sigma-plus-u state. Both potentials dissociate to a pair of ground-state cesium atoms. The vibrational splittings of these two potentials are incommensurate, and the large mass of cesium yields a high density of states. The ultracold cesium atoms have a temperature of approximately 100 microkelvin. The atoms are cooled and confined in a dark SPOT magneto-optic trap. The atoms are optically pumped into the 6s1/2 F equals mF equals 4 state. The photoassociation laser excites the atoms into a bound state of the Cs2 2Sigma-minus-g potential. The excited state decays to a manifold of a3Sigma-plus-u vibrational levels, which are ionized by a pulsed laser. A second probe laser searches for resonances between the desired a3Sigma-plus-u levels and the excited 2Sigma-minus-g level. The binding energy is reported relative to the hyperfine barycenter located approximately 8.04 GHz below the asymptote. The total spin of the pair of cesium nuclei is denoted I, and the total electron spin is S. The hyperfine interaction splits levels with different f according to the given formula with A approximately equal to 2.3 GHz. The rotational energy splits states with different l by the rotational constant Bv approximately equal to 0.1 GHz. The pairs of cesium atoms in the spin-polarized sample have f equals mf equals 8, and only pairs with l equals 0 are excited. The PA laser has sigma-plus polarization, so electric dipole selection rules ensure F prime equals mF prime equals 9. The global fit of the potentials to all known levels in both states took into account the second-order spin-orbit interaction. The potentials for spectral regions with insufficient data were modeled using the Hannover analytic form. The root-mean-square deviation was approximately 90 MHz for sublevel splittings and approximately 200 MHz for absolute binding energies. The typical experimental uncertainties were approximately 30 MHz for sublevel splittings and approximately 400 MHz for absolute binding energies.

Procedures And Architectures
The photoassociation laser excites the atoms into a bound state of the Cs2 2Sigma-minus-g potential dissociating to the 6s1/2 plus 6p3/2 asymptote. The probe laser frequency is scanned while monitoring the ion yield to look for resonant dips in the signal. The difference between the frequencies of the resonant probe and PA lasers gives the binding energy of the a3Sigma-plus-u level. The use of PA levels in the pure long-range well of the 2Sigma-minus-g state enables access to deeply bound a3Sigma-plus-u levels. The Hund's case c 2Sigma-minus-g excited state has resolved levels of definite J prime, where J prime equals l prime plus S prime plus L prime. The PA laser is tuned to excite only J prime equals 2 levels, which are a mixture of l prime equals 0, 2, 4. The electric dipole selection rules for the probe transition ensure that only a3Sigma-plus-u states with I equals 7 and l equals 0, 2, 4 are detected. The global fit of the potentials to all known levels in both states took into account the second-order spin-orbit interaction. The level positions and line strengths qualitatively agree with predictions based on the a3Sigma-plus-u long-range potential. The observed degeneracy is between the a3Sigma-plus-u level and the X1Sigma-plus-g level assigned as the X1Sigma-plus-g state. The microwave field could drive transitions between sublevels of the a3Sigma-plus-u and X1Sigma-plus-g states. A magnetic dipole transition can be driven between the observed level and the X state level at approximately 6.3 GHz. An electric dipole transition can be driven between the observed level and the X state level at approximately 9.8 GHz. The linewidth of approximately 1 Hz could be achieved using a manner like that used for atomic fountain clocks. One measurement every 2 seconds with signal-to-noise of 100 yields a linewidth uncertainty of approximately 5 times 10 to the power of negative 5 Hz in one day. The energy sensitivity is approximately 5 times 10 to the power of 12 Hz for transitions of this type. The atomic fountains achieve a signal-to-noise of approximately 1000 every approximately 1.3 seconds.

Key Results
The maximum value of the energy sensitivity is obtained for levels with energy approximately equal to three-quarters of the dissociation limit. The energy sensitivity is only slightly diminished from its expected value in the harmonic approximation at the maximum. The energy sensitivity for close-lying X and a state levels is much smaller than for the X state alone. The energy sensitivity increases monotonically with the binding energy throughout the region of a state levels. The search for variation of mu will be most sensitive when using nearly-degenerate levels lying as close as possible to the a state minimum. Multiple sublevels were observed for several a3Sigma-plus-u vibrational levels with binding energies between 400 and 1500 GHz. The level positions and line strengths qualitatively agree with predictions based on the a3Sigma-plus-u long-range potential. The sublevels for each vibrational level are clustered together according to their f value. The single accessible a3Sigma-plus-u level has mixed strongly with a nearby X1Sigma-plus-g level only in this vibrational state. The perturbing level is assigned as the X1Sigma-plus-g state with vibrational number 138. The degeneracy is between the deeply bound a3Sigma-plus-u level and the X1Sigma-plus-g level in Cs2. The magnetic dipole transition between the observed level and the X state level occurs at approximately 6.3 GHz. The electric dipole transition between the observed level and the X state level occurs at approximately 9.8 GHz. The transition amplitude for the electric dipole transition is approximately 1.5 times 10 to the power of negative 4 times the elementary charge times the Bohr radius. The root-mean-square deviation was approximately 90 MHz for sublevel splittings and approximately 200 MHz for absolute binding energies. The fractional change of delta mu over mu less than or equal to 10 to the power of negative 17 could be achieved in approximately one day. The required accuracy is only about ten times less than the best atomic clocks. The relative change of the splitting requires only about ten times less accuracy than the best atomic clocks. The near-degeneracies at energies where the energy sensitivity is considerably larger await further data for confirmation.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The harmonic potential provides a general mechanism for amplifying the absolute size of the energy sensitivity. The v-fold enhancement arises because the energy sensitivity scales with the vibrational quantum number. The density of states becomes large near the dissociation limit, so the energy sensitivity becomes small for the highest levels. The scheme uses the much larger energy sensitivity for states of intermediate vibrational excitation. The overlapping potentials with incommensurate vibrational splittings create near-degeneracies that enhance sensitivity. The strong hyperfine mixing reduces the energy sensitivity for the directly observed X state sublevel. The unobserved X state sublevels can be accurately predicted for use in the proposed experiment. The proposed measurement requires only about ten times less accuracy than the best atomic clocks. The system is promising for future searches for small variations in mu. The near-degeneracies at energies where the energy sensitivity is considerably larger await further data for confirmation.

Contradictions And Limitations
The analysis assumes both the electron mass and alpha remain constant, which is equivalent to using a reference clock based on optical atomic transitions. The strong hyperfine mixing reduces the energy sensitivity for the directly observed X state sublevel. The transitions between sublevels are nominally forbidden, requiring microwave or magnetic dipole driving. The near-degeneracies at energies where the energy sensitivity is considerably larger await further data for confirmation. The details of the data and the fit will be given elsewhere, indicating incomplete reporting. The level assignments are tentative, based on global fits and qualitative agreement with predictions. The paper notes that during preparation, two papers exploring similar ideas in other systems were learned of. The systematic errors associated with astrophysical measurements are difficult to eliminate due to uncertainty in the sources. The assumption of constant alpha and electron mass is a simplification that may not hold in all models. The predicted sensitivity depends on conservative assumptions that may not reflect actual experimental conditions.

Three Takeaways
The core contribution is the proposal of laboratory experiments using molecular vibrational levels for enhanced sensitivity to variation of mu.
